hints: Focus on the actual nucleophilic addition mechanism, not just the overall equation, and ask what forms right after cyanide attacks the carbonyl.
Draw the intermediate as $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{O}^-)\text{CN}$ and check the four groups on the central carbon for chirality and where the charge sits.
Remember that any species with a full negative charge and lone pairs can donate electrons, then decide if that makes it both basic and nucleophilic.
walkthrough:
**Recall the catalysed mechanism**

The catalyst provides $\text{CN}^-$, a strong nucleophile. It attacks the partially positive carbonyl carbon in $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CHO} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{O}^-)\text{CN}$$

**Identify the intermediate structure**

The intermediate is an alkoxide ion, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{O}^-)\text{CN}$. The negative charge is localised on the oxygen atom.

So statement 2 is correct, there is a single negative charge on O.

**Test for chirality**

Look at the central carbon in the intermediate. It is bonded to four different groups: $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{H}$, $\text{O}^-$, and $\text{CN}$.

Four different groups means a chiral centre, so each intermediate molecule formed is chiral. Statement 1 is correct.

**Decide if it is a nucleophile**

A nucleophile is an electron pair donor. The $\text{O}^-$ has three lone pairs and a full negative charge, so it is electron rich.

In the next step it donates a pair to $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{HCN}$ to form $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$ and regenerate $\text{CN}^-$. Acting as a base in this step still means it is nucleophilic in character. Statement 3 is correct.

**Combine the statements**

Since 1, 2 and 3 are all correct, the combination for all three is the right choice.

options.A: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 3 are all true. The alkoxide intermediate $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{O}^-)\text{CN}$ has four different groups on carbon so is chiral, carries one negative charge on oxygen, and with its lone pairs and negative charge is a nucleophile (which acts as a base toward HCN).
options.B: Incorrect. This combination includes only 1 and 2. Students choose this if they think the intermediate cannot be a nucleophile because its job is to accept a proton. A proton acceptor (base) with lone pairs is still classed as electron rich and nucleophilic.
options.C: Incorrect. This combination includes only 2 and 3. Students choose this if they think the intermediate is achiral. Check again: central C has $\text{H}$, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CN}$ and $\text{O}^-$, four different groups, so it is chiral.
options.D: Incorrect. This combination includes only 1. Students choose this if they confuse the intermediate with the $\text{CN}^-$ catalyst or forget the alkoxide $\text{O}^-$ carries the negative charge and lone pairs that make statements 2 and 3 true.
